description: CAD bake-off 2 of 3 -- BUILD123D: build the SO-101 gripper assembly parametrically in cad/build123d/. SHARED CONTEXT (same task, three tools, one pebble each so they can run in separate git worktrees): recreate the SO-101 gripper assembly -- the fixed jaw (gripper body) and the moving jaw -- as a baseline for comparing three CAD tools. Jake verbatim: "I want to be able to modify them in the future, so you will have to do it in a way that supports that." That means parametric, editable source. Importing a mesh and calling it done FAILS the test. Use named variables for every dimension that might plausibly change: jaw length, jaw opening, fingertip thickness, servo horn bore, fastener sizes, wall thickness. DIMENSIONAL SOURCE OF TRUTH -- two real SO-101 STEP files are already committed at cad/build123d/reference/: Moving_Jaw_SO101.step and Wrist_Roll_Follower_SO101.step. STEP carries exact analytic geometry, so measure from these. Do NOT re-download them and do NOT invent or eyeball dimensions from tessellated meshes. WHY THIS PART: it is what Jake will modify for the Hand 1.0 paper gripper -- cross-reference plans/hand_1_0.md and plans/gripper_bet.md as reading, and cite them in your notes. DELIVERABLE BESIDES THE MODEL: a NOTES.md in your own tool directory covering time taken, what was easy, what was painful, whether the tool known weakness actually mattered in practice, and how it would feel to modify this part six months from now. State plainly if the geometry ends up approximate and list what still needs verifying. BOUNDARIES: stay inside your own cad/<tool>/ directory and touch nothing else. Do NOT edit plans/hand_1_0.md or plans/gripper_bet.md -- a later pass writes the comparison across all three tools. The other two tool pebbles are running in parallel in their own worktrees, so do not touch cad/openscad/, cad/build123d/, or cad/blender/ other than your own. TOOL SPECIFICS: a Python venv already exists at cad/build123d/.venv (gitignored) -- REUSE it, do not reinstall or recreate it. build123d is Python, parametric, and real B-rep, so exercise exactly what it is supposed to be better at: import the reference STEP as B-rep (cad/build123d/reference/Moving_Jaw_SO101.step and Wrist_Roll_Follower_SO101.step, already in this directory) and take real measurements off the analytic geometry; put genuine fillets on edges; export BOTH a STEP and an STL. Commit the script, the exports, and a render if you make one. Leave the reference/ STEP files themselves unmodified. KNOWN DOWNSIDE TO EVALUATE HONESTLY IN NOTES.md: dependency footprint -- a venv plus OCCT versus a single self-contained file. Was that a real cost here, and does it change over six months of edits? MID-FLIGHT CLARIFICATION (added 2026-09-13, AFTER this pebble was claimed and work had started -- read it even if you are already mid-run; it changes what you optimize for, not what you build): WHY WE ARE DOING THIS (the goal is not the gripper -- the goal is choosing the tool). Recreating a part that already exists produces nothing new on its own. Its entire value is as a controlled benchmark. Jake is about to design Hand 1.0 (a paper-handling gripper that mounts to the SO-101 and is also usable handheld) and later Hand 2.0 (a fully 3D-printed human hand identical to its teleop glove). That is a long hardware design programme and it should be done in ONE tool. This exercise decides which one. WHY RECREATE A KNOWN PART SPECIFICALLY: because there is ground truth. The reference STEP files say exactly what the geometry should be, so "did this tool let me express the real part accurately" has a checkable answer -- unlike designing something new, where any result looks plausible and you learn nothing about the tool. WHAT IS ACTUALLY BEING MEASURED (optimize for producing a fair verdict, NOT for finishing fast): (1) Can this tool express real mechanical geometry accurately, from measured dimensions? (2) How painful is it to change a dimension six months later? This matters MORE than initial build speed, because these parts will be iterated many times against measurements that do not exist yet. (3) Does it live well in git -- readable diffs, reviewable history? (4) Can an AGENT author and revise it directly? Jake wants to iterate hardware by voice, which means the format has to be text an agent can reliably write. (5) Is the output actually usable for functional printed parts -- fits, fillets, fasteners, bearing seats? (6) It must be open source. That was Jake's stated requirement. THEREFORE: an honest NOTES.md verdict is the PRIMARY deliverable, equal in value to working geometry. An agent that hits a genuine wall and documents it precisely has done this task correctly. Do NOT paper over friction to make your tool look good -- a tool that loses fairly here saves months of pain later. This decision feeds plans/hand_1_0.md (section 6 records the provisional OpenSCAD-first call that this exercise is meant to confirm or overturn) and plans/gripper_bet.md -- read both, cite them, and still do not edit them. FOR BUILD123D SPECIFICALLY: this is the strongest challenger on criteria (1) and (5) -- real B-rep, real fillets, STEP in and out -- so judge it hardest on (2), (3) and (4): are Python diffs readable in git, and can an agent reliably author and revise this by voice six months from now? Weigh that against the dependency footprint honestly in both directions.
test_instructions: cad/build123d/ contains a parametric Python model with named parameters for jaw length, jaw opening, fingertip thickness, servo horn bore, fastener sizes and wall thickness
The script imports the reference STEP as B-rep and dimensions are measured from it rather than invented
Real fillets are applied, and both a STEP and an STL export are committed
The existing cad/build123d/.venv was reused, not recreated, and reference/*.step are unmodified
cad/build123d/NOTES.md covers time, easy, painful, whether the dependency-footprint downside mattered, six-month modifiability, and what still needs verifying
Nothing outside cad/build123d/ is modified -- in particular plans/hand_1_0.md and plans/gripper_bet.md are untouched

results.identified_issue:
CAD bake-off tool 2 of 3. Deliverables in cad/build123d/: params.py (every
dimension named and tagged [STEP]/[DERIVED]/[FITTED]/[ASSUMED]),
measure_reference.py (interrogates the reference B-rep, writes MEASUREMENTS.md),
moving_jaw.py + fixed_jaw.py, gripper.py (assembly + STEP/STL + drawings),
fidelity_check.py (writes FIDELITY.md), edit_stress.py, build.sh, NOTES.md.

METHOD. Loaded both reference STEP files with import_step (0.19 s each) and
measured analytic surfaces via BRepAdaptor_Surface: exact cylinder radii and
axes, exact plane normals and offsets, torus minor radii. Cross-sections via
`solid & Plane(...)` gave the tapering blades station by station. Nothing was
eyeballed off a mesh. Both blades are lofts through those measured stations,
one loft segment per step of the gripping face, so the station tables in
params.py ARE the silhouette.

RESULT (FIDELITY.md, both shapes compared in the same kernel): moving jaw
-2.4% volume, worst silhouette error 0.27 mm; follower +2.9% volume, bounding
boxes within 0.2 mm on every axis.

FAILURE MODES A FUTURE AGENT SHOULD KNOW, all OCCT:
1. fillet() with a radius that does not fit first raises
   "BRep_API: command not done", then on retry SEGFAULTS (exit 139) — no
   traceback, no partial result. moving_jaw._fillet_where_possible() tries a
   descending radius list and keeps only a result that passes is_valid. Net
   effect: fillet radius is a wish, not a parameter; it degrades silently.
2. is_valid is NOT sufficient. Lofting the moving jaw to its real 0.8 mm tip
   returned is_valid==True with volume -1.665e11. Only comparing volume to the
   reference caught it. The loft now stops at y=-81.8 and is filleted.
3. A "successful" fillet can leave an invalid shell whose crash surfaces much
   later, inside project_to_viewport (HLR). Cut holes BEFORE filleting.
4. Boolean against the imported reference (model - reference) silently returns
   the whole operand — OCCT declining to cut against the reference's B-spline
   faces. That is why fidelity_check compares cross-sections, not a boolean.
5. extrude(profile, amount=+n) on Plane(x_dir=(0,1,0), z_dir=(1,0,0)) extruded
   along -X. The cut missed the part entirely and everything still built,
   validated and rendered plausibly; only the cross-section area table caught
   it (762 mm2 expected, 871 mm2 actual). Strongest argument for keeping a
   numeric check in every build.
6. ExportSVG crashes (assert start != end in svgpathtools) on a degenerate
   ellipse for some view directions.
7. Detecting "is this cylindrical face a hole" via TopAbs_REVERSED works on an
   imported STEP but not on a freshly built solid; fidelity_check uses the
   geometric normal-vs-axis test instead.

APPROXIMATIONS, all listed in NOTES.md: cosmetic B-spline blends not
reproduced (the originals carry 26 and 34 spline faces); the follower's servo
pocket back face (WR_CAVITY_X0) is FITTED to match measured cross-section
areas, not read off a plane; a gusset under the follower base plate is missing
(9.5 mm silhouette error at z=3, the worst in the model); the Ø10 bore now
breaks into that fitted pocket; the moving jaw tip stops 0.2 mm short.

ASSEMBLY CAVEAT worth escalating: the two STEP files carry no assembly
constraints, so the mate is reasoned, not measured. And it cannot be right as
drawn — the moving jaw's fork gap is 36.4 mm while the follower is 48 mm wide
at that height, so the fork cannot straddle the body. Either a third part sits
between them or the mating surfaces are not the ones I assumed.

CONTAMINATION DISCLOSURE for whoever writes the three-way comparison: partway
through I read the first 120 lines of cad/openscad/params.scad to calibrate
scope, after taking my own measurements but before writing params.py. My
numbers were measured independently and agree with theirs where they overlap,
but the bake-off is not perfectly blind on my side.

Boundaries honoured: nothing outside cad/build123d/ touched, reference/*.step
byte-identical, the existing .venv reused (nothing installed).
results.summary: Built the SO-101 gripper in build123d from measurements taken off the reference STEP, and wrote the honest verdict in cad/build123d/NOTES.md.
results.detailed_description:
Both parts are built in cad/build123d/ from dimensions measured off the reference STEP as real B-rep — exact cylinder radii and plane normals, never off a mesh. The blades are lofted through measured cross-sections, so the station tables in params.py are the silhouette: edit a row and the shape follows. STEP and STL exports, drawings and an assembly are committed.

I also scored it, because both shapes live in the same kernel: the moving jaw is 2.4% under the original by volume with a worst silhouette error of 0.27 mm, the follower 2.9% over, every bounding box within 0.2 mm. FIDELITY.md has the table.

NOTES.md is the real deliverable and it is not a puff piece. build123d earned its dependency — it is the only tool here that could measure the reference and export STEP — but OCCT is a hostile runtime: a fillet that does not fit segfaulted the process with no traceback, and is_valid returned True on a solid whose volume was negative. My recommendation is build123d for the printable parts, on the condition that every model keeps a numeric check that runs on each build. A wrong-direction extrude silently cut nothing and still rendered fine; only the cross-section table caught it.

Two things to look at. The assembly mate is a guess and it cannot be right as drawn — the moving jaw's fork gap is 36.4 mm and the follower is 48 mm wide there, so the fork cannot straddle the body; something is missing from my reading. And one disclosure: partway through I read part of the OpenSCAD pass's params file to calibrate scope, after taking my own measurements, so my side of the bake-off is not perfectly blind.
